Subject: Warm-standby RTO/RPO clarifications needed

Kimberly —

Thanks for the initial questionnaire. Two follow-ups from our architects so we can complete the procurement package:

1) For warm-standby across two regions, what are the realistic RTO and RPO targets we should expect for a standard Redwood Managed model (no custom quantization changes)? Please provide both median and worst-case numbers (with assumptions).

2) During failover, what parts of the authentication/CBAC flow need manual intervention vs. automated routing? Our security team needs a brief sequence of steps.

3) Evidence request: we need a sample runbook extract that shows the switchover steps and the post-failover validation checklist (sanity checks, data-consistency verification). A short PDF excerpt is fine.

Appreciate a response by EOD Monday if possible — procurement timeline is tight.

Hi Lisa —

Thanks for the clear asks. I pulled together a concise response and an excerpt from our recovery playbook. High level answers below; full runbook excerpt attached.

1) RTO / RPO for Redwood Managed (warm-standby):
- Typical (median) effective RTO: 8-12 minutes for control-plane routing + 15-30 minutes for full KV cache warm-up depending on traffic profile.
- Worst-case observed RTO (no manual escalation): 45-90 minutes (this assumes cross-region capacity ramp, DNS TTL propagation if configured, and cold cache rebuild for long-tail sessions).
- Typical RPO: near-zero for metadata and user-generated inputs when using async replication; estimated potential token-loss window < 30s under streaming workloads, up to 5 minutes in extreme network partition scenarios where tail-end batching is pending.

Assumptions: active traffic is small-to-medium variance, model variants are pre-provisioned in second region (warm instances available), prefix caching is enabled, and cross-region replication for metadata is set to <5s. We can tighten numbers with a dedicated reserved pool.

2) Authentication & CBAC during failover:
- Automated: routing policy shift, model endpoint promotion, backend connection rebinds (within our control plane).
- Manual required (typical): scoped network peering toggles or manual route updates if customer's firewall/VPN uses static restrictions; temporary rekeying only in rare compliance-triggered incidents.
- Sequence (short): 1) Detect failover trigger (automated monitor or ops), 2) Promote warm pool in DR region (automated if autoscale policy triggered), 3) Update routing rules and CDN/edge config (automated for cloud-based routing; manual review for on-prem VPC peering), 4) Verify KMS access and token exchange flows, 5) Execute post-failover validation.

3) Runbook excerpt: attached (RM_DR_Playbook_v3.pdf) — includes step-by-step switchover and the minimal post-failover checks we recommend (trace validation, token-level latency sampling, embedded payload checksum, and spot-eval using golden prompts).

We can also run a tabletop/demo failover with your team next week. Is Wednesday afternoon PST feasible for a 60-min run?

Thanks —
Kimberly Park
Enterprise Solutions — Redwood Inference

Kimberly / Marcus / Grace —

Looping in ops and pricing to add the two items Tom requested. Draft notes below; Kimberly can polish and send to HorizonMed.

1) Warm instance billing model (summary):
- Option A: Ephemeral warm pool (recommended for proofs/short-term coverage) — warm instances are billed at a reduced standby rate (approximately 15-30% of active inference rate depending on instance type) with metered activation minutes for full throughput. No minimum commitment; suitable for customers who want lower ongoing costs but flexible failover.
- Option B: Reserved warm capacity (recommended for predictable SLAs) — monthly commitment for reserved GPU capacity; unit economics are better for sustained traffic and guarantees capacity for sub-10m RTO in most scenarios.

Cost-impact note (to include in reply): "Warm ephemeral pools reduce standby cost by ~70-85% compared to fully provisioned active capacity; reserved pools commit X units/month and reduce activation latency variability." (we'll add specific numbers based on the instance family selected).

2) Firewall checklist (two-line sample for HorizonMed network team):
- Allow egress from HorizonMed CIDR to redwood-inference-edge.<region>.redwood.ai on TCP 443 and UDP 3478 (STUN) for edge connectivity; maintain outbound NAT for session affinity.
- Ensure inbound management access from our control-plane IP ranges (listed in the full playbook) is permitted for KMS verification and health-check probes during failover windows.

Grace / Marcus — can one of you attach the warm-standby evidence bundle (sanity test logs + recovery validation run) and a short paragraph on how tokens were validated during the last rehearsal?

Thanks,
Vivek
Head of Customer Reliability — Redwood Inference

Lisa / Tom —

Per your requests, attached is the compact response bundle: short billing note, network checklist, and the runbook excerpt. Key items below for quick paste into your acceptance criteria: 

- SLA / RTO commitment (example acceptance language): "Redwood Inference will provide warm-standby capacity that enables an average switchover (control-plane routing + KV cache warm-up) of 10-20 minutes under normal operating conditions, with documented mitigation steps for extended recovery up to 90 minutes."

- RPO acceptance note: "Redwood’s cross-region replication provides near-zero metadata loss for control-plane artifacts. During failover streaming workloads, token loss is expected to be negligible (typical <30s); customers can opt for synchronous replication (reserved pools) to minimize this window further."

- Cost-impact blurb (for procurement): "Ephemeral warm pools bill at reduced standby rates (approx. 15-30% of active inference cost) with metered activation minutes; reserved warm capacity requires monthly commitment and offers improved latency predictability and lower per-minute activation cost."

- Network checklist (paste-ready):
1) Allow egress from HorizonMed VPC CIDR to redwood-inference-edge.us-west-2.redwood.ai on TCP/443 and UDP/3478.
2) Permit inbound management access from Redwood control-plane IP ranges (documented in the playbook) for KMS and health check validation during failover.
3) If using firewall-based peering, have an on-call contact and escalation window (15 minutes) to approve temporary route changes; otherwise prefer cloud-routing policies to avoid manual intervention.

Attachments: RM_DR_Playbook_v3.pdf, warm-standby-evidence.tar.gz (includes sanity-run logs, token-validation snapshots, and a 30-minute rehearsal report).

We can convert the acceptance language into a short addendum for your contract if that helps accelerate procurement. Let us know and we’ll draft. Also confirming Wednesday next week we have a 60-min tabletop at 1400 PST if that still works — I'll send a calendar invite.

Best,
Kimberly Park
